bracket: [Textbook error in this worked example, CORRECTED below rather than preserved, because a printed worked solution is a method a student copies. The question asks in which \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) bond the inductive effect is least; the book's printed solution answers "the bond between carbon-3 and hydrogen", which is a \(\text{C}-\text{H}\) bond — so as printed the solution does not answer its own question. The correct answer follows from the book's OWN principle, stated in the same sentence, that the effect diminishes as the number of intervening bonds increases: of the two \(\text{C}-\text{C}\) bonds this molecule has, \(\text{C}_1-\text{C}_2\) and \(\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3\), the further from the bromine on \(\text{C}_1\) is \(\text{C}_2-\text{C}_3\).]

[Textbook misprint in part (d), which does not balance in carbon. The reactant \((\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C}-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\) has FIVE carbons (three methyls, a quaternary carbon and the \(-\text{CH}_2\text{OH}\)), while the product as printed, \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBrCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\), has SIX. The rearranged five-carbon product this reaction actually gives is \((\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CBr}-\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3\) (2-bromo-2-methylbutane), formed by a methyl shift to the primary carbocation. The classification the question asks for is unaffected — it is a rearrangement either way, since the carbon skeleton changes and the product is a tertiary rather than a primary bromide — so the answer below stands on the reaction as intended.]
